newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Exiles threaten violence in China's Moslem region.
newsitem.headline: Exiles threaten violence in China's Moslem region.

text.p: Uighur exiles said on Thursday that only violence would end Chinese rule in remote Xinjiang and they forecast more unrest in Beijing's mainly Moslem northwestern province.

Alleging Beijing intended on Thursday to execute two Uighur students who were arrested after riots in Xinjiang last month, about 35 young ethnic Uighurs staged a noisy protest demonstration outside the Chinese Embassy in Almaty, capital of neighbouring Kazakhstan.
The protesters shouted "East Turkestan!", the Moslem Uighurs' name for their province, and "Allahu akbar!" (God is great).
Anxious Chinese diplomats darted about the small crowd in front of the embassy building of fading yellow stucco filming protesters with video recorders and cameras.
"They (China) want to shoot more of our people," said one of the demonstrators, Malik Vasilov, 28. "There will be an armed struggle -- the Uighur people have lost patience with the Chinese."
Officials in Xinjiang said on Thursday they had indicted six people in connection with anti-Chinese rioting in the province who could face the death sentence if convicted.
But they denied Uighur exile allegations that China would execute two rioters on Thursday.

The riots in Yining, near the border with Kazakhstan, were some of worst in the province, home to a majority of Turkic-speaking Moslems like the ethnic Uighurs, since the communists took power in 1949.
Exile groups have said the riots were sparked by the execution of about 30 Uighurs by the Chinese authorities. Chinese sources said nine people were killed and 198 wounded in the disturbances.
News from the region of lonely mountain passes and treacherous desert -- described by one traveller as "a very abomination of desolation" -- seeps out with traders crossing the China-Kazakh border.
Uighur exiles say telephone links to Xinjiang have been restored but their information is difficult to verify.
The exiles say events in Xinjiang, which means New Frontier in Chinese, are set to take a more violent turn.
"No state supports us, we have no guns," said a Uighur from Yining, who fled to Kazakhstan after the riots and who did not want to be identified. "We only have terrorism."
A string of bus bombings shook the regional capital Urumqi following the Yining riots, killing nine and wounding 74.
Chinese officials have said there is no evidence linking the Uighurs to a bus bombing in Beijing earlier this month but the have heightened security in the Chinese capital.
The Yining Uighurs say underground groups, like "Cheraq", or "Spark", recently decided to take their armed struggle to the rest of China. They say Uighurs were behind the Beijing bomb.

Exiles in Almaty say China's "assimilation" policy, the closure of many mosques in the province -- often the focus of Uighur separatist activity -- and a large Chinese military presence could see Uighur patience snap, with violent consequences.
The former Soviet countries abutting Xinjiang -- which share a Turkic language, Islam and a nomadic heritage -- have also stoked Uighur hopes of establishing their own state.

"We will fight the Chinese as the Chechens fought the Russians," said one of the men from Yining, who said he threw rocks at Chinese soldiers during the riots but who said he was now scared to return.
